Show that ABCD is a rectangle. *(3 Marks — Moderate)* **Answer** Given: ABCD is a parallelogram, so $AD \parallel BC$ and $AD = BC$ (opposite sides). Also given: $AC = BD$. **Proof** In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle BAD$: - $AB = BA$ (common side) - $AC = BD$ (given) - $BC = AD$ (opposite sides of parallelogram $ABCD$) $$\triangle ABC \cong \triangle BAD \quad \text{(SSS congruence)}$$ $$\Rightarrow \angle DAB = \angle CBA \qquad \dots(i) \text{ [CPCT]}$$ Since $AD \parallel BC$ and $AB$ is a transversal, the co-interior (allied) angles on the same side add to $180°$: $$\angle DAB + \angle CBA = 180° \qquad \dots(ii)$$ From (i) and (ii): $\angle DAB + \angle DAB = 180° \Rightarrow 2\angle DAB = 180°$ $$\angle DAB = \angle CBA = 90°$$ Since one angle of parallelogram $ABCD$ is $90°$, and a parallelogram with one right angle has all four angles equal to $90°$ (co-interior angles being supplementary forces every angle to $90°$ in turn), ABCD is a rectangle. (Proved) --- ## Question 2 **Question:** Show that the diagonals of a square are equal and bisect each other at right angles. *(3 Marks — Moderate)* **Answer** Let $ABCD$ be a square. Diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $O$. **Part 1 — Diagonals are equal** In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle BAD$: - $AB = BA$ (common) - $\angle ABC = \angle BAD = 90°$ (angles of a square) - $BC = AD$ (sides of a square) $$\triangle ABC \cong \triangle BAD \quad \text{(SAS)} \Rightarrow AC = BD \quad \text{[CPCT]}$$ **Part 2 — Diagonals bisect each other at right angles** Since a square is a parallelogram, its diagonals bisect each other, so $OB = OD$. In $\triangle AOB$ and $\triangle AOD$: - $AO = AO$ (common) - $AB = AD$ (sides of square) - $OB = OD$ (diagonals of square bisect each other) $$\triangle AOB \cong \triangle AOD \quad \text{(SSS)} \Rightarrow \angle AOB = \angle AOD \quad \text{[CPCT]}$$ But $\angle AOB$ and $\angle AOD$ form a linear pair: $$\angle AOB + \angle AOD = 180° \Rightarrow 2\angle AOB = 180° \Rightarrow \angle AOB = 90°$$ Hence $AC = BD$, and $AC \perp BD$ with $O$ the mid-point of both — the diagonals of a square are equal and bisect each other at right angles. (Proved) --- ## Question 3 **Question:** ABCD is a parallelogram in which diagonal AC bisects $\angle A$ (see figure). Show that (i) it bisects $\angle C$ also, (ii) ABCD is a rhombus. *(4 Marks — Hard)* **Answer** Given: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram, and diagonal $AC$ bisects $\angle A$, i.e. $\angle DAC = \angle BAC$. **(i) AC bisects $\angle C$** Since $AB \parallel DC$ and $AC$ is a transversal: $$\angle BAC = \angle DCA \quad \text{(alternate interior angles)} \qquad \dots(a)$$ Since $AD \parallel BC$ and $AC$ is a transversal: $$\angle DAC = \angle BCA \quad \text{(alternate interior angles)} \qquad \dots(b)$$ But $\angle DAC = \angle BAC$ (given, AC bisects $\angle A$) $\qquad \dots(c)$ From (a), (b), (c): $\angle DCA = \angle BAC = \angle DAC = \angle BCA$ $$\Rightarrow \angle DCA = \angle BCA$$ So AC bisects $\angle C$ as well. **(ii) ABCD is a rhombus** We now have $\angle BAC = \angle BCA$ (from the chain above). These are the two base angles of $\triangle ABC$ standing on side $AC$, at vertices $A$ and $C$ respectively. Equal angles have equal opposite sides: $$\angle BAC = \angle BCA \Rightarrow BC = AB \quad \text{(side opposite } \angle BAC \text{ is } BC\text{; opposite } \angle BCA \text{ is } AB\text{)}$$ Since $ABCD$ is a parallelogram, its opposite sides are equal: $AB = CD$ and $BC = AD$. Combining with $AB = BC$ just found: $$AB = BC = CD = AD$$ All four sides of $ABCD$ are equal, so ABCD is a rhombus. (Proved) --- ## Question 4 **Question:** ABCD is a rectangle in which diagonal AC bisects $\angle A$ as well as $\angle C$. Show that (i) ABCD is a square, (ii) diagonal BD bisects $\angle B$ as well as $\angle D$. *(4 Marks — Hard)* **Answer** Given: $ABCD$ is a rectangle, so $\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = \angle D = 90°$ and $AB = DC$, $BC = AD$. Diagonal $AC$ bisects both $\angle A$ and $\angle C$. **(i) ABCD is a square** In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ADC$: - $\angle BAC = \angle DAC$ (AC bisects $\angle A$) - $\angle BCA = \angle DCA$ (AC bisects $\angle C$, and since $AB \parallel DC$, $\angle BCA=\angle DAC$ while $\angle DCA = \angle BAC$ by alternate angles — consistent with the bisector condition) - $AC = AC$ (common) $$\triangle ABC \cong \triangle ADC \quad \text{(ASA)} \Rightarrow AB = AD \quad \text{[CPCT]}$$ Since $ABCD$ is a rectangle, $AB = DC$ and $AD = BC$. Combined with $AB = AD$ just shown: $$AB = BC = CD = DA$$ A rectangle with all four sides equal is a square, so ABCD is a square. **(ii) Diagonal BD bisects $\angle B$ and $\angle D$** In $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle CBD$: - $AB = CB$ (sides of the square, just proved equal) - $AD = CD$ (sides of the square) - $BD = BD$ (common) $$\triangle ABD \cong \triangle CBD \quad \text{(SSS)}$$ $$\Rightarrow \angle ABD = \angle CBD \quad \text{[CPCT]} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \angle ADB = \angle CDB \quad \text{[CPCT]}$$ So diagonal BD bisects both $\angle B$ and $\angle D$. (Proved) --- ## Question 5 **Question:** ABCD is a parallelogram, and points $P$ and $Q$ are taken on diagonal $BD$ such that $DP = BQ$ (see figure). Show that (i) $\triangle APD \cong \triangle CQB$ (ii) $AP = CQ$ (iii) $\triangle AQB \cong \triangle CPD$ (iv) $AQ = CP$ (v) $APCQ$ is a parallelogram. *(5 Marks — Hard)* **Answer** Given: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram; $P, Q$ lie on diagonal $BD$ with $DP = BQ$. **(i) $\triangle APD \cong \triangle CQB$** In $\triangle APD$ and $\triangle CQB$: - $DP = BQ$ (given) - $\angle ADP = \angle CBQ$ (since $AD \parallel BC$ with transversal $BD$, alternate interior angles $\angle ADB = \angle DBC$) - $AD = CB$ (opposite sides of parallelogram $ABCD$) $$\triangle APD \cong \triangle CQB \quad \text{(SAS congruence)}$$ **(ii) $AP = CQ$** $$AP = CQ \quad \text{[CPCT, from part (i)]}$$ **(iii) $\triangle AQB \cong \triangle CPD$** In $\triangle AQB$ and $\triangle CPD$: - $BQ = DP$ (given) - $\angle ABQ = \angle CDP$ (since $AB \parallel CD$ with transversal $BD$, alternate interior angles $\angle ABD = \angle CDB$) - $AB = CD$ (opposite sides of parallelogram $ABCD$) $$\triangle AQB \cong \triangle CPD \quad \text{(SAS congruence)}$$ **(iv) $AQ = CP$** $$AQ = CP \quad \text{[CPCT, from part (iii)]}$$ **(v) APCQ is a parallelogram** From parts (ii) and (iv): $AP = CQ$ and $AQ = CP$ — both pairs of opposite sides of quadrilateral $APCQ$ are equal. A quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides equal is a parallelogram, so APCQ is a parallelogram. (Proved) --- ## Question 6 **Question:** ABCD is a parallelogram and $AP$ and $CQ$ are perpendiculars from vertices $A$ and $C$ on diagonal $BD$ (see figure). Show that (i) $\triangle APB \cong \triangle CQD$ (ii) $AP = CQ$. *(3 Marks — Moderate)* **Answer** Given: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram, $BD$ its diagonal, $AP \perp BD$ at $P$ and $CQ \perp BD$ at $Q$. **Solution** Since $AB \parallel DC$ and $BD$ is a transversal: $$\angle ABD = \angle CDB \quad \text{(alternate interior angles)} \qquad \dots(i)$$ In $\triangle APB$ and $\triangle CQD$: - $\angle APB = \angle CQD = 90°$ (given, both are perpendiculars) - $\angle ABP = \angle CDQ$ (same as $\angle ABD = \angle CDB$ from (i), as $P, Q$ lie on $BD$) - $AB = CD$ (opposite sides of parallelogram $ABCD$) $$\triangle APB \cong \triangle CQD \quad \text{(AAS congruence)}$$ (i) $\triangle APB \cong \triangle CQD$ (Proved) $$\Rightarrow AP = CQ \quad \text{[CPCT]}$$ (ii) $AP = CQ$ (Proved) --- ## Question 7 **Question:** ABCD is a trapezium in which $AB \parallel CD$ and $AD = BC$ (see figure). Show that (i) $\angle A = \angle B$ (ii) $\angle C = \angle D$ (iii) $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle BAD$ (iv) diagonal $AC$ = diagonal $BD$. *(Note: this question is Ex. 8.1's own Q7 — the source worksheet mislabels it "12" and prints it immediately after Q6, having skipped the median-triangle question that normally occupies slot 7; it is renumbered here to match the exercise's own sequence, and the genuine Q12 — a separate MCQ on rhombus conditions — appears later at its correct position. The source figure for this question also mislabels its bottom-left vertex "B" — a duplicate of the top-left vertex — corrected here to "D" to match the vertex order $A,B,C,D$ and the given $AD = BC$.)* *(3 Marks — Moderate)* **Answer** Given: $ABCD$ is a trapezium with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AD = BC$. **Construction** Extend $AB$ to a point $E$, and through $C$ draw $CE \parallel AD$, meeting the extension of $AB$ at $E$ (shown in the figure above). **(i) $\angle A = \angle B$** Since $AD \parallel CE$ and $AE$ (i.e. line $AB$ extended) is a transversal, $ADCE$ is a parallelogram (both pairs of opposite sides parallel: $AD \parallel EC$ by construction, $AE \parallel DC$ since $AB \parallel DC$). So: $$AD = CE \quad \text{(opposite sides of parallelogram } ADCE\text{)}$$ But $AD = BC$ (given), so $BC = CE$, making $\triangle BCE$ isosceles: $$\angle CBE = \angle CEB \quad \text{(angles opposite equal sides)} \qquad \dots(1)$$ Since $\angle ABC$ and $\angle CBE$ form a linear pair: $$\angle ABC + \angle CBE = 180° \Rightarrow \angle CBE = 180° - \angle ABC \qquad \dots(2)$$ Also, since $AE \parallel DC$ with transversal $EC$: $\angle A + \angle CEB = 180°$ (co-interior angles), i.e. $\angle CEB = 180° - \angle A$. Substituting into (1): $180° - \angle ABC = 180° - \angle A$ $$\Rightarrow \angle A = \angle B \quad \text{(i.e. } \angle ABC\text{)}$$ **(ii) $\angle C = \angle D$** Since $AB \parallel CD$ (given), for transversal $AD$: $\angle A + \angle D = 180°$ $\dots(a)$, and for transversal $BC$: $\angle B + \angle C = 180°$ $\dots(b)$ (co-interior angle pairs on each side of the trapezium). From (a) and (b): $\angle A + \angle D = \angle B + \angle C$. But $\angle A = \angle B$ (proved in part (i)), so: $$\angle D = \angle C \quad \Rightarrow \quad \angle C = \angle D$$ **(iii) $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle BAD$** In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle BAD$: - $AB = BA$ (common) - $\angle A = \angle B$ (proved above, i.e. $\angle DAB = \angle CBA$) - $BC = AD$ (given) $$\triangle ABC \cong \triangle BAD \quad \text{(SAS congruence)}$$ **(iv) Diagonal AC = diagonal BD** $$AC = BD \quad \text{[CPCT, from part (iii)]}$$ Hence in trapezium ABCD with AD = BC: $\angle A=\angle B$, $\angle C=\angle D$, $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle BAD$, and diagonal AC = diagonal BD. (Proved) --- ## Question 8 **Question:** This question has an Assertion (A) and a Reason (R). Choose the correct option. **Assertion (A):** The opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal. **Reason (R):** If a quadrilateral's opposite sides are equal and parallel, then it is a parallelogram. (a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. (b) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A. (c) A is true, but R is false. (d) A is false, but R is true. *(1 Mark — Moderate)* **Answer** Both statements need to be checked independently, and then whether R logically explains A. **Checking A** Opposite angles of a parallelogram are indeed always equal (a standard, true property of every parallelogram). So A is true. **Checking R** "If a quadrilateral's opposite sides are equal and parallel, it is a parallelogram" — this is also a true statement; it is one of the standard tests for a quadrilateral to be a parallelogram. **Does R explain A?** R describes a *criterion for identifying* a parallelogram (a sufficient condition for a quadrilateral to be one) — it does not, by itself, explain *why opposite angles are equal*. The actual reason opposite angles are equal comes from congruent triangles formed by a diagonal (as in Q1's proof method), which is a different argument from R. So R, although true, is **not** the correct explanation of A. Correct option: (b) — both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. --- ## Question 9 **Question:** The diagonals of a parallelogram: (a) are never equal (b) are equal (c) bisect each other (d) are perpendicular to each other *(1 Mark — Easy)* **Answer** This is a basic, always-true property of every parallelogram (not just special cases like rectangles or rhombuses). Diagonals being *equal* (option b) is true only for rectangles/squares — not all parallelograms. Diagonals being *perpendicular* (option d) is true only for rhombuses/squares. But every parallelogram's diagonals **bisect each other** — this follows directly from $\triangle AOB \cong \triangle COD$ (using $AB=CD$, alternate angles from $AB \parallel CD$). Correct option: (c) — the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. --- ## Question 10 **Question:** Consider the two statements below and choose the correct option: (i) A square is a parallelogram. (ii) A square is a rhombus. (a) Only (i) is true. (b) Only (ii) is true. (c) Both (i) and (ii) are true. (d) Both (i) and (ii) are false. *(1 Mark — Easy)* **Answer** A square satisfies the definitions of several quadrilateral families at once. A square has both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal — so it is indeed a parallelogram. A square also has all four sides equal — so it is also a rhombus (a parallelogram with all sides equal). Both statements hold simultaneously. Correct option: (c) — both (i) and (ii) are true. --- ## Question 11 **Question:** Match the quadrilateral in Column A with its identifying property in Column B, and choose the correctly matched option. | Column A | Column B | |---|---| | 1. Rectangle | (i) Opposite sides are equal and parallel | | 2. Parallelogram | (ii) Diagonals are equal | | 3. Square | (iii) Diagonals bisect each other at right angles | | 4. Rhombus | (iv) All sides are equal and every angle is $90°$ | (a) $1\to(ii), 2\to(i), 3\to(iv), 4\to(iii)$ (b) $1\to(ii), 2\to(iv), 3\to(i), 4\to(iii)$ (c) $1\to(ii), 2\to(iii), 3\to(iv), 4\to(i)$ (d) $1\to(i), 2\to(ii), 3\to(iii), 4\to(iv)$ *(1 Mark — Moderate)* **Answer** Match each shape to the property that is genuinely its own distinguishing feature (beyond the basic parallelogram properties every one of them already has). - Rectangle's extra, defining feature beyond being a parallelogram: **equal diagonals** → (ii) - Parallelogram's basic defining property: **opposite sides equal and parallel** → (i) - Square's defining feature: **all sides equal AND every angle $90°$** → (iv) - Rhombus's extra, defining feature: **diagonals bisect each other at right angles** → (iii) Correct option: (a) — $1\to(ii), 2\to(i), 3\to(iv), 4\to(iii)$. --- ## Question 12 **Question:** Choose the correct option from below. A parallelogram is a rhombus, if (i) all its sides are equal. (ii) its opposite angles are equal. (iii) its diagonals bisect each other at right angles. (iv) all its angles are $90°$. (a) (i) and (iii) both are true. (b) (i) and (ii) both are true. (c) (iii) and (iv) both are true. (d) only (iv) is true. *(1 Mark — Moderate)* **Answer** Check each statement against what genuinely characterises a rhombus among parallelograms. (i) All sides equal — this is exactly the definition of a rhombus. **True.** (ii) Opposite angles equal — true for every parallelogram (not special to rhombus), so this alone doesn't make it a rhombus, but as a *statement* about a rhombus it's still true — however it is not one of the two selected as the answer since the standard characterisation pairs (i) with (iii). (iii) Diagonals bisect each other at right angles — a proven equivalent condition for a parallelogram to be a rhombus (shown by isosceles triangles formed at the intersection point). **True.** (iv) All angles $90°$ — this describes a rectangle, not a rhombus (unless it's also a square). Not a general rhombus property. Both (i) and (iii) are genuine, standard equivalent conditions for a parallelogram to be a rhombus. Correct option: (a) — (i) and (iii) both are true. --- ## Question 13 **Question:** Read the two statements below, and then choose the correct option from the alternatives given. (i) The diagonals of a parallelogram are always equal. (ii) A trapezium is always a parallelogram. (a) Only (i) is true. (b) Only (ii) is true. (c) Both (i) and (ii) are false. (d) Both (i) and (ii) are true. *(1 Mark — Moderate)* **Answer** Test each statement against a general (non-special) example. (i) Take any parallelogram that is *not* a rectangle (e.g. a "slanted" parallelogram) — its diagonals are clearly of different lengths. So diagonals are equal only for rectangles/squares, not every parallelogram. **False.** (ii) A trapezium has only ONE pair of parallel sides by definition; a parallelogram needs BOTH pairs of opposite sides parallel. A general trapezium (with non-parallel, unequal legs) is not a parallelogram at all. **False.** Correct option: (c) — both (i) and (ii) are false. --- ## Question 14 **Question:** The diagonals of a rhombus intersect at $90°$, and each diagonal bisects: (a) only one angle. (b) all the angles. (c) only two angles. (d) none of the angles. *(1 Mark — Easy)* **Answer** A rhombus's diagonals have a stronger property than an ordinary parallelogram's. Each diagonal of a rhombus splits a pair of opposite vertex angles into two equal halves — since a rhombus is symmetric about each diagonal (all sides equal makes the triangles on either side of a diagonal congruent by SSS). This holds for both diagonals, at all four vertices. Correct option: (b) — the diagonals of a rhombus bisect all the (vertex) angles. --- ## Question 15 **Question:** Which property is true for BOTH a rhombus and a rectangle? (a) All sides are equal. (b) All angles are equal. (c) The diagonals bisect each other. (d) The diagonals are perpendicular to each other. *(1 Mark — Easy)* **Answer** Both a rhombus and a rectangle are special parallelograms, so check which property is inherited from being a parallelogram (common to both), versus which is a special feature unique to only one of them. "All sides equal" is special to rhombus only. "All angles equal ($90°$)" is special to rectangle only. "Diagonals perpendicular" is special to rhombus only. But "the diagonals bisect each other" is a property of **every parallelogram**, so it holds for both a rhombus and a rectangle (since both are parallelograms). Correct option: (c) — the diagonals bisect each other, in both a rhombus and a rectangle.

paperQuestions/smL2oECzfafprH0erLzs.question: ABCD এটা আয়তক্ষেত্ৰ য'ত কৰ্ণ AC এ $\angle A$ আৰু $\angle C$ দুয়োটাকে সমদ্বিখণ্ডিত কৰে। দেখুওৱা যে (i) ABCD এটা বৰ্গক্ষেত্ৰ, (ii) কৰ্ণ BD এ $\angle B$ আৰু $\angle D$ দুয়োটাকে সমদ্বিখণ্ডিত কৰে।
paperQuestions/smL2oECzfafprH0erLzs.answer: দিয়া আছে: $ABCD$ এটা আয়তক্ষেত্ৰ, সেয়ে $\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = \angle D = 90°$ আৰু $AB = DC$, $BC = AD$। কৰ্ণ $AC$ এ $\angle A$ আৰু $\angle C$ দুয়োটাকে সমদ্বিখণ্ডিত কৰে। **(i) ABCD এটা বৰ্গক্ষেত্ৰ** $\triangle ABC$ আৰু $\triangle ADC$ ৰ পৰা: - $\angle BAC = \angle DAC$ (AC এ $\angle A$-ক সমদ্বিখণ্ডিত কৰে) - $\angle BCA = \angle DCA$ (AC এ $\angle C$-ক সমদ্বিখণ্ডিত কৰে, আৰু $AB \parallel DC$ হোৱাত একান্তৰ কোণ হিচাপে $\angle BCA=\angle DAC$ আৰু $\angle DCA = \angle BAC$ — সমদ্বিখণ্ডিতৰ চৰ্তৰ সৈতে সংগতিপূৰ্ণ) - $AC = AC$ (সাধাৰণ) $$\triangle ABC \cong \triangle ADC \quad \text{(ASA)} \Rightarrow AB = AD \quad \text{[CPCT]}$$ $ABCD$ আয়তক্ষেত্ৰ হোৱাত, $AB = DC$ আৰু $AD = BC$। $AB = AD$ ৰ সৈতে মিলাই: $$AB = BC = CD = DA$$ চাৰিওটা বাহু সমান হোৱা আয়তক্ষেত্ৰ এটা বৰ্গক্ষেত্ৰ, সেয়ে ABCD এটা বৰ্গক্ষেত্ৰ। **(ii) কৰ্ণ BD এ $\angle B$ আৰু $\angle D$ সমদ্বিখণ্ডিত কৰে** $\triangle ABD$ আৰু $\triangle CBD$ ৰ পৰা: - $AB = CB$ (বৰ্গৰ বাহু, ওপৰত প্ৰমাণিত) - $AD = CD$ (বৰ্গৰ বাহু) - $BD = BD$ (সাধাৰণ) $$\triangle ABD \cong \triangle CBD \quad \text{(SSS)}$$ $$\Rightarrow \angle ABD = \angle CBD \quad \text{[CPCT]} \qquad \text{আৰু} \qquad \angle ADB = \angle CDB \quad \text{[CPCT]}$$ সেয়ে কৰ্ণ BD এ $\angle B$ আৰু $\angle D$ দুয়োটাকে সমদ্বিখণ্ডিত কৰে। (প্ৰমাণিত)
